text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

When people discuss what's going to happen next in broker consolidation, Arthur J Gallagher is often overlooked. In sixth place in the list of the world's largest brokers as a result of other big mergers, Gallagher is now looking for opportunities to expand.
Market talk has it that Gallagher is now considering trying to fill the shoes worn by Johnson & Higgins in the UNISON insurance alliance, before J&H was bought by Marsh & McLennan.

The other partners of UNISON have so far not made clear their future intentions, although the French member Gras Savoye recently sold a major stake to UK broker Willis Corroon which is set to lead to closer co-operation. Jauch & Huebener remains particularly vulnerable having lost its international network and with its former ally now a part of the group that owns its major rival.

Gallagher is understood to have been in talks with UNISON members, and it may well be that some new form of the alliance could emerge. International coverage is a weak spot for Gallagher, and an international partnership could be of great benefit to it.

Gallagher is also looking at the possibility of acquisitions. These are unlikely to be on the same grand scale as its larger rivals, but recently Gallagher has been no slouch in the field of purchases.

In addition to last year's purchase of a majority interest in Sydney, Australia, based National Risk Control Services, Gallagher used 1,115,000 of its common shares to acquire five brokerage firms and an investigation services firm.

Those included Levitt/Kristan Co. of Los Angeles; Phoenix-based Alliance Insurance Group; Lamberson Koster & Co. of San Francisco; Morgan, Read & Coleman (Holdings) Ltd. and Morgan Insurance Services Ltd. of London; Pasadena, California-based R.W. Stephens & Co and Florida-based Beymer & Bond Investigations Inc.
So far this year, Gallagher has acquired Colorado-based Byerly & Co and Michigan-based Arnold & Co, both employee benefit consulting businesses.
Also this year, Gallagher divested itself of an office in Atlanta, selling it to Willis Corroon.
In approaching mergers, Gallagher is likely to be looking at the opportunities they bring for expanding the company's operations, rather than trying to capitalise on economies of scale.

Gallagher could yet be the target of a merger bid itself. Potential candidates are not obvious, but the Gallagher family has reduced its ownership from 100 percent to only 20 percent. With respectable earnings of over $250 million and some new business picked up from consolidation fall-out set to push profits up, the idea cannot be dismissed lightly.
